comparison: Perfect agreement on slip boundary condition analysis (C33, C34). Both evaluations find this work SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the 'good discussion of the role of slip' as part of comprehensive physical reasoning.

Perfect agreement on network geometry independence (C35, C36). Both evaluations find this work SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note 'good use of imaging to represent ER network geometries' and the comprehensive nature of the analysis.

Both address the main conclusion (C75) but with different evaluation types. OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED based on systematic computational exploration. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, noting the work is 'solely theoretical' and 'main conclusions await experimental validation' despite finding the theoretical analysis convincing.

Strong agreement on perinuclear sheet spatial decay findings (C52, C53, C67). Both evaluations find this work SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers describe the work as 'carefully and comprehensively conducted' with no specific critiques of this analysis. Peer result also includes C8 not in OpenEval result.

Both address peripheral sheet contractions (C54, C55) and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval focuses on biological plausibility of contraction rates. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'contraction of peripheral sheets provides a much more credible mechanism' and praise energy budget analysis (C56 in peer result).

Both address core computational findings about tubule pinching mechanism. OpenEval (C24-C29, C31-C32) finds Péclet number analysis and simulation-experiment comparison SUPPORTED. Peer result (C7, C25, C28, C29, C32, C63-C65) affirms 'convincing evidence' that tubular contraction is unlikely, with substantial overlap on claims C25, C28, C29, C32.

Both address physical principles underlying the analysis. OpenEval covers broader computational findings (C24-C29, C31-C32) while peer result focuses on Péclet number and flow effects (C26, C27, C31). Both find work SUPPORTED with peer reviewers praising 'good use of underlying physical principles' and 'tractable and transparent calculations.'

Both address mixing simulations and negative results. OpenEval (C37, C63-C65) finds the mechanistic explanation SUPPORTED. Peer result includes these claims (C63-C65) plus broader context (C7, C25, C28, C29, C32) and affirms the evidence is convincing that tubular contraction is unlikely.

Both address parameter exploration. OpenEval (C7, C66) focuses on extreme parameter requirements. Peer result (C37, C66, C68) covers broader parameter space exploration. Both find work SUPPORTED with peer reviewers noting 'comprehensive' analysis with 'clear physical arguments.'

Both address junction contraction simulations. OpenEval (C48, C68) finds the 8× faster contraction requirement makes mechanism biologically implausible but SUPPORTED as analysis. Peer result includes C68 among broader parameter exploration (C37, C66, C68), all SUPPORTED.

Both address structural measurements from network reconstruction (C78, C79). OpenEval finds these measurements SUPPORTED as quantitative characterization. Peer result groups these with volume estimates (C48, C81, C82) and praises 'good use of imaging' and 'sensible approximations.'

Both address experimental volume estimates (C81, C82). OpenEval finds methodology reasonable and SUPPORTED despite relying on intensity-volume assumptions. Peer result groups these with structural measurements (C78, C79, C48) and treats them as reliable inputs, all SUPPORTED.

Both address force estimates and energetic feasibility (C69, C70, C71). OpenEval finds physical plausibility arguments SUPPORTED. Peer result includes these claims plus C83-C84 and specifically praises 'analysis of energy budgets' providing 'useful bounds.'

Both address energetic regimes for tubules versus sheets (C83, C84). OpenEval finds physical reasoning sound and SUPPORTED. Peer result groups these with force calculations (C69-C71) and praises 'clear physical arguments' and energy budget analysis.

Both address energetic feasibility of peripheral sheets. OpenEval (C56-C58) focuses on ATP estimates and comparisons to biological motors. Peer result (C9, C54-C56) emphasizes peripheral sheets as 'much more credible mechanism' with overlap on C56. Both find work SUPPORTED.
